title: Treating the complex as complicated
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart uses Helen Timperley's distinction between complicated and complex problems to question the conventional school improvement plan. The typical plan picks three priorities, sets measurable targets and maps actions, which Hart argues treats a complex, interdependent system as if it could be broken into separately solvable parts. He offers three reasons leaders fall into this: inherited received wisdom about how schools improve, an accountability system that rewards tangible artefacts such as RAG-rated action plans, and the limits of a leader's stage of ego development. As an alternative he proposes that principals focus improvement on three interconnected fundamentals: relational trust, problem solving and professional learning. He anticipates the charge of genericism by arguing that domain-specific knowledge supplies the substance of all three, with middle leaders bringing subject specificity. The post ends with a sketch of a 'complex' improvement model built on those priorities and protection from initiative fatigue.
points: Hart shows that a standard improvement plan silently assumes easily identified causes, known solutions, predictable results and separable parts, all features of complicated rather than complex problems.
He argues that the busyness of complicated improvement work can function mainly as reassurance to governors, or to leaders themselves, that something is being done.
Citing Neil Gilbride, he links a leader's grasp of complexity to their stage of ego development, placing plan-driven improvement in the 'self aware' stage.
His alternative priorities are trust, problem solving and professional learning, on the premise that student achievement cannot improve before colleagues' expertise does.
He answers the genericism objection by noting that trust depends on competence and problem solving on domain knowledge, so subject leaders supply the specifics.
quotes: We set a measurable target, map out some actions and then get on with the planned work. This is a pretty good example of treating the complex as if it were complicated.

When current leaders cut their teeth under the tutelage of leaders before them, they pick up received wisdom about how to go about the work. And there are plenty of successful schools out there where leaders may well attribute success to their (complicated) approach to school improvement.

Tangible artefacts such as school improvement priorities that seek to address perceived weakness and the associated RAG rated action plans might give some sort of reassurance that leaders are acting. When there is urgency to improve, the busyness of such complicated school improvement can be the thing that provides reassurance to ourselves or to others that we’re doing our job.

Neil Gilbride argues that the stage of a leader’s ego development affects what they are aware of and can describe, reflect upon and do. Pertinent here is our understanding of complexity, which develops at each stage of ego development.

However, it is domain specific knowledge that provides the substance of building trust, solving problems and supporting others’ learning. After all, a significant factor in trust dynamics is competence; problem solving requires a great deal of domain specific knowledge; and effective professional learning helps participants to build knowledge.

If we select school improvement priorities with such specificity as ‘improving writing’, we fall into the trap of treating the complex as complicated. However, if our school improvement priorities are holistic, cohesive concepts whose absence halts any improvement, such as trust, problem solving and professional learning, we are more likely, I would argue, to take at least one more step away from complicated leadership and one step towards complex leadership.
